issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Thomas, a 53-year-old bus driver, had spent over two decades navigating the crowded streets of his city, but since that night two years ago, every turn and every stop felt like a minefield. On a routine evening shift, he had been assaulted in a dark alley, a traumatic experience that left him feeling utterly powerless. The memory of that night haunted him, the terror he felt replaying in his mind like an old film on a loop. Whenever he dared to recall the event, the same visceral fear washed over him, as if he were reliving the horror in real time. The sounds—the shouts, the scuffle—echoed in his head, and he found himself feeling tired and exhausted by the sheer weight of it all. Driving his bus had become particularly challenging since the assault. The presence of passengers, especially strangers, triggered a deep-seated anxiety. He could feel his heart race as he recalled the encounter, and the slightest noise would send him spiraling back to that night. Each time a trigger jolted him, it would pull forth the memories of the assault, amplifying the sensations of panic and helplessness as if he were right back in the alley, unable to escape the horror. The sudden sound of laughter or a loud voice would send him spiraling back into the memories of the terror, making every detail of that night flood his mind, as though he were reliving the chaos in real time. Each time he was reminded of the assault, whether by a loud voice or a sudden movement, memories of the fear and chaos would flood back, dragging him deeper into the anguish of that moment. He avoided eye contact with his passengers, believing that they could see the shame etched on his face. The shame he felt had transformed into a heavy cloak he wore daily, making him feel as if he could never escape the judgment of others or himself. This belief that he was forever marked by the assault colored his recollections, making the memories sharper and more vivid, reinforcing the idea that he was weak and unworthy. In the quiet moments between stops, he often pondered how he had lost faith in people, convinced that no one could be trusted anymore. This conviction that he was unworthy of trust made even the slightest interactions feel dangerous, as he interpreted gestures and words through a lens of suspicion that heightened his anxiety. This pervasive mistrust seeped into his interactions, making every colleague and passenger a potential threat, a reminder of his own vulnerability. His belief that he couldn't trust anyone meant that even the most innocuous interactions, like a colleague's friendly greeting, felt like a confirmation of danger, triggering an immediate sense of anxiety and wariness. The shame and mistrust he experienced were intertwined with his memories, each reinforcing the other. When he thought about the assault, he was engulfed by a sense of body shame, as if the very essence of his being had been tarnished. Because these memories surged so vividly, he became hyper-aware of his own presence, avoiding mirrors and reflective surfaces, fearing that the sight of himself would trigger another wave of shame and self-doubt. He believed he had let himself down, and that feeling of inadequacy fueled his desire to withdraw from others. In the bus yard, he would often choose to keep to himself, isolating himself from conversations and camaraderie among his fellow drivers. He had come to believe that by avoiding people, he could somehow shield himself from the overwhelming feelings of exposure and vulnerability. Yet this isolation only deepened the cycle of his distress, leading him to feel even more exhausted and drained. As time passed, the triggers became more pronounced. Driving with others was particularly challenging; he felt as though he was being scrutinized, judged for his past, and that made him anxious. The sound of laughter or even casual conversation among passengers felt like an affront, a stark reminder of the joy he could no longer access. Because those memories of joy were intertwined with the horror of his experience, they became triggers that heightened his sense of vulnerability, making him retreat further into silence. Each shift was a test of his endurance, and he often found himself retreating into silence, fearing that any moment could lead him back to the terror he so desperately wanted to avoid. He was aware that his negative appraisals of himself and others were distorting his reality, but he felt powerless to change them. Each time he told himself he was weak or flawed, it seemed to bring the memories of the assault closer, reinforcing the vividness of those moments and making the recall feel even more immediate and painful. Whenever he was reminded of the assault, the memories surged forth, making him hyper-aware of every interaction, and causing him to perceive danger in ordinary life situations, as if every moment was a potential repeat of his trauma. Memories of the assault invaded his thoughts, and he felt trapped in a cycle where triggers led him to recall painful moments, which in turn reinforced his negative beliefs about himself and the world. "His negative appraisals led him to see even benign actions as potential threats, making the world around him feel more fraught, heightening his sensitivity to any reminder of his trauma." As the memories surged back, he became hyper-vigilant about his surroundings, scanning for any potential triggers, turning mundane situations into sources of dread, as if they were reminders of his past trauma. His conviction that he was constantly being judged made even minor triggers—like a loud laugh or a sudden movement—feel like signs of impending threat, reinforcing his negative outlook on the world around him. "This cyclical pattern made him hyper-vigilant, as he became acutely aware of how the memories of that night shifted his perception of ordinary life, turning even mundane situations into potential threats." This thought spiral left him feeling trapped, and he often questioned whether he would ever be able to trust again or find solace in his daily life. It was ultimately the cumulative weight of his struggles that brought Thomas to seek help. He had reached a breaking point where the exhaustion of managing his symptoms overshadowed any semblance of normalcy. He hoped that therapy could help him reclaim the parts of his life that had been stolen, but he was also terrified—terrified of revisiting the pain, of confronting the memories, and of allowing himself to trust anyone ever again. The fear of reliving his trauma clashed with a yearning for liberation, leaving him standing at the precipice of change, unsure of where to step next. "This often left him feeling that he was marked by weakness, and the conviction that he was forever changed made those memories sharper, reinforcing his belief that he could never be safe or whole again." "His belief that he was unworthy meant that even the most benign interactions felt like confirmations of his inadequacy, making him hyper-aware of every glance or whisper, each one a reminder of his perceived flaws." "This lack of trust meant that even familiar faces became sources of anxiety, as he anticipated judgment or betrayal, interpreting their actions through a lens of suspicion that left him on edge." "Consequently, when memories of the assault resurfaced, they would trigger a rush of shame, causing him to shrink back even further, as if he could hide from both the world and the truth of his own experience." "Haunted by the belief that he could never escape the trauma, he longed for a way to break free from the relentless cycle of fear and shame that held him captive." "The sudden sound of laughter or a loud voice would transport him back to that night, as if the trigger had unlocked a door to the past, flooding his mind with vivid images of fear and chaos." violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly convey that triggers influence or lead to memory recall.
The vignette does not establish that negative appraisals influence or lead to triggers.
There is no clear connection showing that memory influences or leads to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not clearly convey that triggers influence or lead to memory recall.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not establish that negative appraisals influence or lead to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: There is no clear connection showing that memory influences or leads to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Thomas, a 53-year-old bus driver, had spent over two decades navigating the crowded streets of his city, but since that night two years ago, every turn and every stop felt like a minefield. On a routine evening shift, he had been assaulted in a dark alley, a traumatic experience that left him feeling utterly powerless. The memory of that night haunted him, the terror he felt replaying in his mind like an old film on a loop. Whenever he dared to recall the event, the same visceral fear washed over him, as if he were reliving the horror in real time. The sounds—the shouts, the scuffle—echoed in his head, and he found himself feeling tired and exhausted by the sheer weight of it all. Driving his bus had become particularly challenging since the assault. The presence of passengers, especially strangers, triggered a deep-seated anxiety. He could feel his heart race as he recalled the encounter, and the slightest noise would send him spiraling back to that night. Each time a trigger jolted him, it would pull forth the memories of the assault, amplifying the sensations of panic and helplessness as if he were right back in the alley, unable to escape the horror. The sudden sound of laughter or a loud voice would send him spiraling back into the memories of the terror, making every detail of that night flood his mind, as though he were reliving the chaos in real time. Each time he was reminded of the assault, whether by a loud voice or a sudden movement, memories of the fear and chaos would flood back, dragging him deeper into the anguish of that moment. He avoided eye contact with his passengers, believing that they could see the shame etched on his face. The shame he felt had transformed into a heavy cloak he wore daily, making him feel as if he could never escape the judgment of others or himself. This belief that he was forever marked by the assault colored his recollections, making the memories sharper and more vivid, reinforcing the idea that he was weak and unworthy. In the quiet moments between stops, he often pondered how he had lost faith in people, convinced that no one could be trusted anymore. This conviction that he was unworthy of trust made even the slightest interactions feel dangerous, as he interpreted gestures and words through a lens of suspicion that heightened his anxiety. This pervasive mistrust seeped into his interactions, making every colleague and passenger a potential threat, a reminder of his own vulnerability. His belief that he couldn't trust anyone meant that even the most innocuous interactions, like a colleague's friendly greeting, felt like a confirmation of danger, triggering an immediate sense of anxiety and wariness. The shame and mistrust he experienced were intertwined with his memories, each reinforcing the other. When he thought about the assault, he was engulfed by a sense of body shame, as if the very essence of his being had been tarnished. Because these memories surged so vividly, he became hyper-aware of his own presence, avoiding mirrors and reflective surfaces, fearing that the sight of himself would trigger another wave of shame and self-doubt. He believed he had let himself down, and that feeling of inadequacy fueled his desire to withdraw from others. In the bus yard, he would often choose to keep to himself, isolating himself from conversations and camaraderie among his fellow drivers. He had come to believe that by avoiding people, he could somehow shield himself from the overwhelming feelings of exposure and vulnerability. Yet this isolation only deepened the cycle of his distress, leading him to feel even more exhausted and drained. As time passed, the triggers became more pronounced. Driving with others was particularly challenging; he felt as though he was being scrutinized, judged for his past, and that made him anxious. The sound of laughter or even casual conversation among passengers felt like an affront, a stark reminder of the joy he could no longer access. Because those memories of joy were intertwined with the horror of his experience, they became triggers that heightened his sense of vulnerability, making him retreat further into silence. Each shift was a test of his endurance, and he often found himself retreating into silence, fearing that any moment could lead him back to the terror he so desperately wanted to avoid. He was aware that his negative appraisals of himself and others were distorting his reality, but he felt powerless to change them. Each time he told himself he was weak or flawed, it seemed to bring the memories of the assault closer, reinforcing the vividness of those moments and making the recall feel even more immediate and painful. Whenever he was reminded of the assault, the memories surged forth, making him hyper-aware of every interaction, and causing him to perceive danger in ordinary life situations, as if every moment was a potential repeat of his trauma. Memories of the assault invaded his thoughts, and he felt trapped in a cycle where triggers led him to recall painful moments, which in turn reinforced his negative beliefs about himself and the world. As the memories surged back, he became hyper-vigilant about his surroundings, scanning for any potential triggers, turning mundane situations into sources of dread, as if they were reminders of his past trauma. His conviction that he was constantly being judged made even minor triggers—like a loud laugh or a sudden movement—feel like signs of impending threat, reinforcing his negative outlook on the world around him. "This cyclical pattern made him hyper-vigilant, as he became acutely aware of how the memories of that night shifted his perception of ordinary life, turning even mundane situations into potential threats." This thought spiral left him feeling trapped, and he often questioned whether he would ever be able to trust again or find solace in his daily life. The fear of reliving his trauma clashed with a yearning for liberation, leaving him standing at the precipice of change, unsure of where to step next. "This lack of trust meant that even familiar faces became sources of anxiety, as he anticipated judgment or betrayal, interpreting their actions through a lens of suspicion that left him on edge." "Consequently, when memories of the assault resurfaced, they would trigger a rush of shame, causing him to shrink back even further, as if he could hide from both the world and the truth of his own experience."
